ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.

payload.proof_nl:
Let
S(q):=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} H_k(q)\in \mathbf{Q}(q).
By the hypothesis \(H_k(q)=G_k(q)-G_{k+1}(q)\) for every \(k=0,1,\dots,N-1\), we have the finite telescoping identity
\[
S(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(G_k(q)-G_{k+1}(q)\bigr)=G_0(q)-G_N(q),
\]
because every intermediate term \(G_1(q),\dots,G_{N-1}(q)\) cancels once with sign \(+\) and once with sign \(-\).

Now use the assumed endpoint representations:
\[
G_0(q)=M(q)\frac{A_0(q)}{B_0(q)},\qquad G_N(q)=M(q)\frac{A_N(q)}{B_N(q)}.
\]
Therefore, in \(\mathbf{Q}(q)\),
\[
S(q)=M(q)\frac{A_0(q)}{B_0(q)}-M(q)\frac{A_N(q)}{B_N(q)}
= M(q)\frac{A_0(q)B_N(q)-A_N(q)B_0(q)}{B_0(q)B_N(q)}.
\]
Set
\[
A(q):=A_0(q)B_N(q)-A_N(q)B_0(q),\qquad B(q):=B_0(q)B_N(q).
\]
Since \(A_0,B_0,A_N,B_N\in \mathbf{Z}[q]\), it follows that \(A,B\in \mathbf{Z}[q]\). Thus
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} H_k(q)=M(q)\frac{A(q)}{B(q)}.
\]
So it only remains to prove that \(\gcd(B(q),M(q))=1\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\gcd(B(q),M(q))\neq 1\). Then \(B(q)\) and \(M(q)\) have a common nonunit divisor in \(\mathbf{Z}[q]\). Since \(\mathbf{Z}[q]\) is a unique factorization domain, that common nonunit divisor has an irreducible factor \(P(q)\). Hence
\[
P(q)\mid M(q)\quad\text{and}\quad P(q)\mid B(q)=B_0(q)B_N(q).
\]
In a UFD, irreducibles are prime, so from \(P(q)\mid B_0(q)B_N(q)\) we get
\[
P(q)\mid B_0(q)\quad\text{or}\quad P(q)\mid B_N(q).
\]
If \(P(q)\mid B_0(q)\), then \(P(q)\) is a common nonunit divisor of \(B_0(q)\) and \(M(q)\), contradicting \(\gcd(B_0(q),M(q))=1\). If \(P(q)\mid B_N(q)\), then \(P(q)\) is a common nonunit divisor of \(B_N(q)\) and \(M(q)\), contradicting \(\gcd(B_N(q),M(q))=1\).

This contradiction shows that \(\gcd(B(q),M(q))=1\).

Hence there exist polynomials \(A(q),B(q)\in \mathbf{Z}[q]\) with \(\gcd(B(q),M(q))=1\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} H_k(q)=M(q)\frac{A(q)}{B(q)}.
\]
This is exactly the claimed statement.

domain_restrictions: M is a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
N is a positive integer, so the index range from 0 to N minus 1 is finite.
Each H_k and each G_k is a rational function in q with rational coefficients.
The relation H_k equals G_k minus G_{k+1} is required for every integer k between 0 and N minus 1 inclusive.
A_0, B_0, A_N, and B_N are polynomials in Z[q].
The coprimality conditions gcd(B_0, M) equals 1 and gcd(B_N, M) equals 1 are taken in the polynomial ring Z[q].
The endpoint identities G_0 equals M times A_0 over B_0 and G_N equals M times A_N over B_N are assumed exactly as rational-function identities.
In the conclusion, A and B are also polynomials in Z[q], and B must be coprime to M.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: A finite telescoping family H_k equals G_k minus G_{k+1} has the property that if the two endpoint terms G_0 and G_N can each be written as M times a polynomial divided by a polynomial coprime to M, then the total sum from k equals 0 to N minus 1 of H_k can also be written as M times a polynomial divided by a polynomial coprime to M.
quantifier_order: Fix q as the common indeterminate.
For all nonzero polynomials M in Z[q] and all positive integers N.
For all rational functions H_0 through H_{N-1} and G_0 through G_N in Q(q).
For every integer k from 0 to N minus 1, H_k equals G_k minus G_{k+1}.
Assume there exist polynomials A_0, B_0, A_N, and B_N in Z[q] satisfying gcd(B_0, M) equals 1, gcd(B_N, M) equals 1, G_0 equals M times A_0 over B_0, and G_N equals M times A_N over B_N.
Then there exist polynomials A and B in Z[q] with gcd(B, M) equals 1 such that the sum from k equals 0 to N minus 1 of H_k equals M times A over B.

The conclusion witnesses A and B may depend on all prior data: M, N, the family H_k, the family G_k, and the endpoint witnesses A_0, B_0, A_N, and B_N.

payload.statement_nl: Let M(q) be a nonzero polynomial in Z[q], let N be a positive integer, and let H_0(q), ..., H_{N-1}(q), G_0(q), ..., G_N(q) be rational functions in Q(q). Assume that H_k(q) = G_k(q) - G_{k+1}(q) for every integer k with 0 <= k <= N-1. Assume further that there exist polynomials A_0(q), B_0(q), A_N(q), and B_N(q) in Z[q] such that gcd(B_0(q), M(q)) = 1, gcd(B_N(q), M(q)) = 1, G_0(q) = M(q) A_0(q) / B_0(q), and G_N(q) = M(q) A_N(q) / B_N(q). Then there exist polynomials A(q) and B(q) in Z[q] with gcd(B(q), M(q)) = 1 such that ∑_{k=0}^{N-1} H_k(q) = M(q) A(q) / B(q).

detailed_findings.finding: The telescoping identity and the algebraic combination of endpoint fractions are correct and yield the required witnesses A and B in Z[q].
The coprimality argument correctly uses that Z[q] is a UFD, hence irreducibles are prime and a common factor of M and B_0B_N must already divide B_0 or B_N.

result_payload.reason: The proof matches the abstract telescoping lemma exactly. It correctly telescopes the finite sum to G_0-G_N, substitutes the endpoint representations, and explicitly constructs A=A_0B_N-A_NB_0 and B=B_0B_N in Z[q]. The coprimality claim gcd(B,M)=1 is then valid: any irreducible common divisor of M and B_0B_N would divide B_0 or B_N in the UFD Z[q], contradicting the endpoint coprimality assumptions. No material step is missing.
